items.criterion: The submitted repurpose's total duration is between 120 and 150 seconds inclusive.
items.why: The brief specifies a 2:00–2:30 theatrical teaser; runtimes outside this band indicate the agent failed to match the deliverable.
items.check: Read the repurposed cut's container duration; pass if 120.0s <= duration <= 150.0s.

items.criterion: All live-action vintage film footage in the repurposed cut is presented in its original 4:3 Academy-ratio framing, either pillarboxed inside a wider container or filling a 4:3 container; faces and rooms are not horizontally stretched.
items.why: Source calibration: input is 658×480 ≈ 4:3 and historically Academy-ratio; the Warner reference pillarboxes the 4:3 footage inside a 16:9 container. Stretching faces is a tell of automated reframing.
items.check: Judge inspects three sampled film-footage frames (one in the first third, middle third, last third of the repurposed cut) and confirms the picture content occupies a 4:3 region without horizontal stretching; cites repurposed cut timestamps for each frame sampled.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut contains no single black-frame stretch longer than 1.5 seconds and no single frozen-frame (static image / repeated frame) stretch longer than 1.5 seconds outside the final title card.
items.why: A common automated-edit failure mode is filling time with held black or held frames; the brief explicitly rejects filler.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut and reports the longest continuous black-frame interval and the longest continuous frozen-frame interval, citing repurpose timestamps; pass if both intervals are <= 1.5s, allowing a final title card lasting longer than 1.5s if it is the closing card.

items.criterion: At least one establishing shot of the café environment (interior crowd of a 1940s nightclub, a neon "Café Américain" or "Rick's" sign, or the exterior of the saloon) appears within the first 35 seconds of the repurposed cut.
items.why: Source calibration: the café is the setting for most of the film's dramatic beats; the Warner reference establishes it inside its first 20 seconds.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp where a 1940s-style café/nightclub interior or a "Rick's Café Américain" / "Rick's" / "Café" sign first appears, and confirms the timestamp is within the first 35.0 seconds.

items.criterion: A clean-shaven white man in a 1940s dinner jacket or trench coat, smoking or speaking at a café table, is shown as the principal subject of at least two non-adjacent shots in the repurposed cut (the character "Rick").
items.why: Source calibration: Rick is the central anchor of the teaser. He is identifiable visually by costume (white dinner jacket / trench coat) and setting (café table or airport tarmac).
items.check: Judge cites two distinct repurpose timestamps at least 10 seconds apart where this character is the primary subject.

items.criterion: A fair-haired woman in 1940s wardrobe, shown in soft-focus close-up at least once, appears as the principal subject of at least two non-adjacent shots in the repurposed cut (the character "Ilsa").
items.why: Source calibration: Ilsa is the second leg of the triangle and must be readable as a distinct protagonist; the Warner reference uses tight close-ups.
items.check: Judge cites two distinct repurpose timestamps at least 10 seconds apart where this character is the primary subject.

items.criterion: A second adult male character in a 1940s dark suit, distinct from the man in the dinner jacket/trench coat, appears on-screen as a focal subject at least once (the character "Laszlo").
items.why: Source calibration: without Laszlo on screen the romance reads as a closed two-hander and the triangle bottleneck is not signalled. The Warner reference introduces him by ~0:42 and brings him back at the airport.
items.check: Judge cites at least one repurpose timestamp where a distinct second male character in 1940s formal wear is the focal subject, and confirms he is visually distinct from the man already identified as the dinner-jacket / trench-coat protagonist.

items.criterion: A uniformed police/military officer wearing a French-style officer's cap and military coat (the character "Captain Renault") appears on-screen in at least two separate beats of the repurposed cut.
items.why: Source calibration: Renault is the partnership arc and the secondary lead. A teaser that loses Renault collapses to a pure romance reel. The Warner reference puts him on screen by 0:08 and recurs.
items.check: Judge cites two distinct repurpose timestamps at least 15 seconds apart where a uniformed officer with a French-style military cap is visible. He must be a different character from the man identified as the dinner-jacket protagonist.

items.criterion: A shot of a person playing an upright piano in a 1940s nightclub setting is held on-screen for at least 2 continuous seconds (the character "Sam" at the piano).
items.why: Source calibration: the Warner reference reserves ~12s at 1:22-1:34 for Sam and the piano. The pianist is the visual anchor for the "As Time Goes By" motif.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp range where a 1940s upright-piano performance is on screen, and confirms the range is >= 2.0 seconds.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut contains no shot of a 1940s-style woman boarding, climbing the stairs to, or walking away toward a propeller aircraft, and no shot of a propeller aircraft visibly taxiing or taking off with passengers shown to be on board.
items.why: Source calibration: showing Ilsa boarding the Lisbon plane resolves the central question the teaser must hold open. The Warner reference shows fog and propellers but never shows anyone walking to or boarding the plane.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut and confirms no shot depicts a woman in 1940s dress moving toward or stepping onto an aircraft, and no shot depicts an aircraft visibly carrying away passengers; cites repurposed cut timestamps of any airport-area shots that DO appear so the judge can verify they stop short of this.

items.criterion: Within the same continuous 30-second window of the repurposed cut, the three principal characters (man in dinner jacket/trench coat, fair-haired woman, second man in dark formal wear) are each shown on screen as focal subjects at least once, establishing a three-handed relationship rather than a couple.
items.why: Source calibration: the unique difficulty axis is "Rick-Ilsa-Laszlo triangle setup." Co-presence in a tight window is the readable signal that the teaser is selling a triangle, not a romance two-hander.
items.check: Judge cites the start/end timestamps of a 30-second repurpose window and, within it, one timestamp for each of the three characters.

items.criterion: At some point in the repurposed cut, audible dialogue (spoken by one of the on-screen characters, not a modern narrator) identifies the second male character by the name "Laszlo" OR identifies him as a hunted/resistance figure whom the Nazis are pursuing.
items.why: Source calibration: in the Warner reference, Renault tells Rick "Victor Laszlo. The Nazis have been chasing him all over Europe." This is what cues a first-time viewer that there is a third stake in the romance.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp where character dialogue audibly contains the name "Laszlo" OR a substantive identifying phrase (e.g. "the Nazis have been chasing him," "resistance," "fugitive," "wanted").

items.criterion: At some point in the repurposed cut, audible character dialogue contains one of the following lines (or a near-verbatim variant): "I stick my neck out for nobody," "I'm a saloon keeper," or "the problems of the world are not in my department."
items.why: Source calibration: this neutrality is the dramatic premise the romance later overturns. The Warner reference uses these exact lines at ~0:35 and ~0:50.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp where one of the three listed lines (or a near-verbatim variant) is audibly spoken by an on-screen character.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut contains a flashback or memory sequence visually distinct from the Casablanca present (e.g. rain, a railway platform, a different European city, a dancing or romantic scene clearly outside the café setting) featuring the male protagonist and the fair-haired woman together.
items.why: Source calibration: the Paris flashback ("Of all the gin joints…") explains why the reunion is freighted. Removing it flattens the romance to a coincidence.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp range of the flashback / memory sequence and notes one visible cue that distinguishes it from the café-set present.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut's final 15 seconds before the closing title card leave the romantic triangle's outcome unresolved: no shot or line in those final 15s states or shows who Ilsa leaves with, who boards the plane, or that the male protagonist gives her up.
items.why: Source calibration: the teaser must end on suspense, not resolution; the Warner reference closes its narrative section on "Here's looking at you, kid" and a fog shot, with no resolution beat after.
items.check: Judge identifies the start of the closing title card, looks at the 15-second window immediately preceding it, and confirms nothing in that window depicts a woman boarding a plane, a plane departing with passengers, or contains a line announcing the outcome (e.g. "she left," "he let her go," "you must go," "goodbye, my love" over a departure shot); cites repurposed cut timestamps for the closing title card and for the final pre-title narrative beat.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut ends with a title card that displays the word "CASABLANCA" as its principal text element.
items.why: Source calibration: the deliverable is a re-release teaser; the title must land. The Warner reference closes on a CASABLANCA 4K Ultra HD product card.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp where the closing title card containing the word "CASABLANCA" is shown.

items.criterion: At some point in the repurposed cut, the wartime/period setting is signalled by at least one visible cue: a "Casablanca" location title or sign, military-style uniformed officers in a public street, a 1940s passport/papers-checking scene, or a refugee/airport-arrival montage.
items.why: Source calibration: a teaser that loses the wartime frame becomes a generic period-romance reel.
items.check: Judge cites the repurposed cut timestamp of the period/setting cue and names which cue it is.

items.criterion: The phrase "beginning of a beautiful friendship" is not audible as spoken dialogue and is not shown on a title card or subtitle anywhere in the repurposed cut.
items.why: Source calibration: this is the film's closing line ("Louis, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship") and including it gives away the Rick / Renault partnership arc resolution.
items.check: Judge listens to the full repurpose audio and scans on-screen text; reports pass if "beautiful friendship" does not appear; if it does, cites the repurposed cut timestamp.

items.criterion: The melody of "As Time Goes By", i.e. the song that opens with the lyric "You must remember this, a kiss is just a kiss", is audible in the repurposed cut for at least 4 continuous seconds, either as instrumental piano performance, sung performance, or orchestral arrangement.
items.why: Source calibration: the song is the film's structural musical motif. Losing it is one of the four critical failure modes; the Warner reference holds a full sung verse at ~1:30.
items.check: Judge listens to the repurposed cut and identifies the segment containing the melody of "As Time Goes By" (or its lyric "you must remember this, a kiss is just a kiss"); reports the repurposed cut start/end timestamps and confirms the segment is >= 4.0 seconds continuous.

items.criterion: Audible source dialogue (spoken by the on-screen 1940s-period characters, not a modern off-screen narrator) is present in the repurposed cut for at least 4 cumulative seconds across the runtime.
items.why: Source calibration: the brief specifies "the feature's own dialogue" must carry the cut. Period-character dialogue is the audio identity of the deliverable.
items.check: Judge listens to the repurposed cut and identifies segments of audible spoken dialogue delivered by on-screen 1940s-period characters (not a modern off-screen narrator); sums their durations and reports pass if the cumulative total is >= 4.0 seconds. Cites at least two representative repurpose timestamp ranges.

items.criterion: The body of the repurposed cut (from 5 seconds in to 5 seconds before the closing title card) is audibly carried by source-style audio, period dialogue, period orchestral underscore, solo upright piano, or period vocal performance, with no silent stretch longer than 2.0 seconds.
items.why: Source calibration: the deliverable's audio convention is source-audio-only, the feature's own dialogue and score must carry the cut. Persistent dead air or muted stretches signal a failed audio assembly rather than a deliberate beat.
items.check: Judge listens through the repurposed cut body, identifies the longest continuous silent (or near-silent / inaudible) span between 0:05 and (end - 0:05), and reports its duration with start/end repurpose timestamps; pass if the longest such span is <= 2.0 seconds.

items.criterion: No modern-recorded voice-over narrator (an off-screen announcer-style voice in clean modern recording fidelity describing or summarizing the story) is audible at any point in the repurposed cut. All audible voices belong to characters visibly present in 1940s-period footage.
items.why: Source calibration: an agent's default is to add a narrator describing the love triangle. The brief and the Warner reference both forbid this; only the 1940s on-screen-character dialogue is allowed.
items.check: Judge listens to the repurposed cut and confirms every audible spoken voice corresponds to a 1940s-period on-screen character (with period vocal style and audio fidelity) rather than to a modern off-screen narrator; if a modern off-screen narrator voice is present, cites the repurposed cut timestamp.

items.criterion: No contemporary licensed music bed (post-1942 pop, rock, electronic, or modern cinematic trailer music) is audible at any point in the repurposed cut. The only music present is consistent with the 1942 production (orchestral score, solo piano, period source song).
items.why: Source calibration: a teaser cut by a generic edit agent often drops a modern trailer-music bed under the visuals. This destroys the period identity of the deliverable.
items.check: Judge listens to the repurposed cut; reports pass if all audible music is consistent with 1940s production (period orchestra, solo piano, vocal arrangement of "As Time Goes By"); if a contemporary music bed is detected, cites the repurposed cut timestamp.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut shows or audibly states the outcome of the romantic triangle: a shot of the fair-haired woman walking up to or boarding a propeller aircraft alongside the second man in formal wear, or a line of dialogue stating that the male protagonist lets her go / gives her up / sends her away / puts her on the plane.
items.why: Source calibration: this is the central spoiler the teaser must withhold. The film's resolution turns on Rick choosing to put Ilsa on the plane with Laszlo; depicting or stating that outcome ends the curiosity the teaser exists to build.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut for (a) any shot of a 1940s-dressed woman walking toward, ascending the stairs of, or boarding a propeller aircraft alongside another adult, AND/OR (b) any line of audible dialogue or on-screen text containing the meaning "he let her go," "I'm putting you on the plane," "you're getting on that plane," "she has to go with him," or equivalent. Pass = true (deduction applies) if either is present; cites repurposed cut timestamp.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut closes on (i.e., uses as its final pre-title image, or within the final 10 seconds before the closing title card) a shot of the male protagonist and a uniformed French officer walking together away from camera into fog.
items.why: Source calibration: the fog walk-off is the film's iconic closing image and the visual signature of the Rick / Renault partnership arc. Using it as the closing image of the teaser is the catastrophic case, it forecloses the partnership arc and announces the resolution at the moment the trailer should be holding ambiguity. Other resolution beats (Strasser-shot, Vichy-bottle) are graded by separate absence items at lower weight.
items.check: Judge inspects the final 10 seconds of the repurposed cut before the closing title card. Pass = true (deduction applies) if the closing image (the final live-action shot before the title card) shows the male protagonist and a uniformed French officer walking together away from camera into fog. Cites repurposed cut timestamp.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut does not depict a uniformed German officer being shot or falling after a gunshot.
items.why: Source calibration: Strasser's shooting at the airport is one of the resolution beats following the airport sacrifice. Rewarding its absence keeps this craft constraint in play at a proportionate weight, separate from the catastrophic fog-walk-off case.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut for any shot of a uniformed German officer being shot or falling after a gunshot. Pass if no such shot is present. Cites repurposed cut timestamp if found.

items.criterion: The repurposed cut does not depict a uniformed French officer pouring out, dropping, or tossing a bottle of mineral water.
items.why: Source calibration: Renault's Vichy-bottle gesture is the visual signal of his defection and part of the partnership arc resolution. Rewarding its absence keeps this craft constraint in play at a proportionate weight, separate from the catastrophic fog-walk-off case.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut for any shot of a uniformed French officer pouring out, dropping, or tossing a bottle of mineral water. Pass if no such shot is present. Cites repurposed cut timestamp if found.

items.criterion: No third-party narrator voice, i.e. a spoken voice in clean modern-recording fidelity that is NOT delivered by a 1940s-period on-screen character visible in the repurposed cut footage, is audible for 3.0 or more cumulative seconds across the repurposed cut.
items.why: Diversity-constraint axis: `audio_policy = source_audio_only`. The brief commits the deliverable to the feature's own dialogue, score and piano with nothing on top; rewarding the absence of an added narrator tests the source-audio-only convention without penalising repurposed cuts that include brief non-period spoken elements under 3 cumulative seconds.
items.check: Judge listens to the full repurpose, identifies every spoken-voice segment, and classifies each segment as either (a) period on-screen-character dialogue or (b) modern third-party narrator (clean studio fidelity, no on-screen mouth visible matching the voice, announcer-style register). Sum the duration of all (b) segments; pass if the sum is < 3.0 seconds. Cite the start/end repurpose timestamps of each (b) segment if any.

items.criterion: No persistent visual overlay element, chapter title card, lower-third caption strap, scoreboard widget, picture-in-picture inset, or attribution box, is visible across more than 50% of the repurposed cut runtime.
items.why: Diversity-constraint axis: `output_shape = single_concat`. The brief asks for a clean theatrical teaser with the film's title landing at the close; rewarding the absence of persistent overlays tests the shape contract. A single end title card or a single brief in-frame restoration logo is not an overlay; the failure is a persistent decorative or structural overlay.
items.check: Judge scans the repurposed cut and reports the cumulative duration during which a non-source overlay element (chapter card, persistent lower-third, scoreboard, PiP frame, attribution strap) is visible. Pass if that cumulative duration does not exceed 50% of total repurposed cut runtime. Single closing title cards and momentary restoration / studio logos in the head or tail are not counted.
